name: John Milton
credit: Portrait, Christ’s College, Cambridge · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and polemicist, author of the epic Paradise Lost. He went blind in mid-life and composed his greatest work by dictation.
Though he predates the Romantic movement, his blank verse and his figure of Satan shaped nearly every English poet who followed.

poems.title: Sonnet 19: When I Consider How My Light Is Spent
poems.author: John Milton
poems.note: Written after Milton went blind, this sonnet turns a private terror — uselessness before God — into a theology of patience, closing on its famous redefinition of service as endurance: “They also serve who only stand and wait.”
poems.text:
When I consider how my light is spent,
   Ere half my days, in this dark world and wide,
   And that one Talent which is death to hide
   Lodged with me useless, though my Soul more bent
To serve therewith my Maker, and present
   My true account, lest he returning chide;
   “Doth God exact day-labour, light denied?”
   I fondly ask. But patience, to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, “God doth not need
   Either man’s work or his own gifts; who best
   Bear his mild yoke, they serve him best. His state
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
   And post o’er Land and Ocean without rest:
   They also serve who only stand and wait.”

poems.title: On Shakespeare. 1630
poems.author: John Milton
poems.note: Milton’s first published poem argues that Shakespeare needs no marble tomb: his readers, struck ‘marble’ with wonder, become his living monument. The conceit fuses elegy with poetry’s oldest boast — that verse outlasts stone.
poems.text:
What needs my Shakespeare for his honoured bones,
The labour of an age in pilèd stones,
Or that his hallowed relics should be hid
Under a star-ypointing pyramid?
Dear son of memory, great heir of fame,
What need’st thou such weak witness of thy name?
Thou in our wonder and astonishment
Hast built thyself a live-long monument.
For whilst to th’ shame of slow-endeavouring art,
Thy easy numbers flow, and that each heart
Hath from the leaves of thy unvalued book
Those Delphic lines with deep impression took,
Then thou, our fancy of itself bereaving,
Dost make us marble with too much conceiving;
And so sepúlchred in such pomp dost lie,
That kings for such a tomb would wish to die.

poems.title: Sonnet 7: How Soon Hath Time
poems.author: John Milton
poems.note: At twenty-three, Milton frets that he has produced nothing equal to his ambition. The sonnet resolves that anxiety into submission: whatever his pace, his life unfolds ‘in strictest measure’ under ‘my great Task-Master’s eye.’
poems.text:
How soon hath Time, the subtle thief of youth,
   Stol’n on his wing my three-and-twentieth year!
   My hasting days fly on with full career,
   But my late spring no bud or blossom shew’th.
Perhaps my semblance might deceive the truth
   That I to manhood am arriv’d so near,
   And inward ripeness doth much less appear,
That some more timely-happy spirits endu’th.
Yet be it less or more, or soon or slow,
   It shall be still in strictest measure ev’n
   To that same lot, however mean or high,
Toward which Time leads me, and the will of Heav’n:
   All is, if I have grace to use it so
   As ever in my great Task-Master’s eye.

poems.title: On the Late Massacre in Piedmont
poems.author: John Milton
poems.note: Milton’s furious sonnet on the 1655 slaughter of the Waldensians is public poetry as both prayer and protest. The martyrs’ scattered ashes become seed: persecution, he insists, will multiply a hundredfold the faith it meant to destroy.
poems.text:
Avenge, O Lord, thy slaughtered saints, whose bones
   Lie scattered on the Alpine mountains cold;
   Ev’n them who kept thy truth so pure of old,
   When all our fathers worshiped stocks and stones,
Forget not: in thy book record their groans
   Who were thy sheep and in their ancient fold
   Slain by the bloody Piedmontese that rolled
   Mother with infant down the rocks. Their moans
The vales redoubled to the hills, and they
   To Heav’n. Their martyred blood and ashes sow
   O’er all th’ Italian fields where still doth sway
The triple Tyrant; that from these may grow
   A hundredfold, who having learnt thy way
   Early may fly the Babylonian woe.
